content: Pennsylvanians were deeply angered, believing that Franklin had consistently supported the Stamp Act, and they even threatened to destroy his home in Philadelphia. Franklin quickly became aware of the widespread colonial resistance to the Stamp Act, and his testimony before the British House of Commons played a significant role in its repeal. This event catapulted Franklin into prominence as the leading advocate for American interests in England. He authored widely read essays supporting the colonies, and Georgia, New Jersey, and Massachusetts also appointed him as their representative to the British Crown. In September 1767, Franklin traveled to Paris with his frequent companion, Sir John Pringle. His groundbreaking electrical discoveries were already well-known in France, earning him introductions to influential scientists, politicians, and even King Louis XV. While living in London in 1768, Franklin developed a phonetic alphabet, outlined in his work A Scheme for a New Alphabet and a Reformed Mode of Spelling. This alphabet eliminated six letters he deemed redundant (c, j, q, w, x, and y) and introduced six new letters for sounds he believed lacked representation. However, this reformed alphabet failed to gain traction, and Franklin eventually abandoned the project. In 1771, Franklin embarked on extensive travels across the British Isles, staying with notable figures such as Joseph Priestley and David Hume. In Dublin, he was invited to sit with members of the Irish Parliament, a rare honor for an American. During his tour of Ireland, Franklin was struck by the severe poverty he witnessed, noting that Ireland's economy suffered under the same restrictive trade regulations and laws imposed by England that governed America. He feared that America could face similar consequences if British colonial exploitation persisted. In 1773, Franklin published two of his most famous pro-American satirical essays: Rules by Which a Great Empire May Be Reduced to a Small One and An Edict by the King of Prussia. He also anonymously co-published an abridgment of the Book of Common Prayer with Francis Dashwood, which included a funeral service reduced to six minutes to preserve the health and lives of the living. Franklin obtained private letters from Massachusetts Governor Thomas Hutchinson and Lieutenant Governor Andrew Oliver, which revealed their encouragement for London to suppress the rights of Bostonians. Franklin sent these letters to America, where they heightened tensions. As a result, Franklin was perceived by the British as a key instigator of colonial unrest. Hopes for a peaceful resolution were dashed when Franklin was publicly ridiculed and humiliated by the Privy Council. He left London in March 1775. By the time Franklin returned to Philadelphia on May 5, 1775, the American Revolution had already begun with the battles of Lexington and Concord. The New England militia had trapped the main British army in Boston. The Pennsylvania Assembly unanimously selected Franklin as their delegate to the Second Continental Congress. In June 1776, he was appointed to the Committee of Five tasked with drafting the Declaration of Independence. Despite being temporarily incapacitated by gout and unable to attend most committee meetings, Franklin made several minor but significant edits to Thomas Jefferson's draft. In December 1776, Franklin was sent to France as a commissioner for the United States. He resided in a home in the Parisian suburb of Passy, provided by Jacques-Donatien Le Ray de Chaumont, a supporter of the American cause. Franklin remained in France until 1785, becoming a beloved figure in French society. Wealthy French families even adorned their parlors with portraits of him. Known for his flirtatious demeanor in the French style, Franklin did not engage in any actual affairs. He successfully managed American diplomatic relations with France, securing a crucial military alliance in 1778 and negotiating the Treaty of Paris in 1783. During his time in France, Franklin, a Freemason, served as Grand Master of the Lodge Les Neuf Sœurs from 1779 to 1781 and was also a Past Grand Master of Pennsylvania. In 1784, Franklin was part of a commission appointed by King Louis XVI to investigate Franz Mesmer's controversial theory of animal magnetism, alongside notable figures such as Antoine Lavoisier, Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, and Jean Sylvain Bailly. When Franklin returned to America in 1785, he was second only to George Washington in his stature as a champion of American independence. Le Ray honored him with a commissioned portrait by Joseph Duplessis, now displayed in the National Portrait Gallery of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C. After his return, Franklin became an abolitionist, freeing his two slaves and eventually serving as president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society. In 1787, he participated as a delegate to the Philadelphia Convention, holding an honorary position and rarely engaging in debates. Franklin is the only Founding Father to have signed all four major documents of the United States' founding: the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, the Treaty of Alliance with France, and the United States Constitution. In 1787, a group of prominent ministers in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, proposed the establishment of a new college named in Franklin's honor. Franklin donated £200 to support the development of what is now Franklin & Marshall College. Between 1771 and 1788, Franklin completed his autobiography, initially addressed to his son but later expanded for the benefit of humanity at the request of a friend. In his later years, as Congress grappled with the issue of slavery, Franklin wrote several essays advocating for the abolition of slavery and the integration of African Americans into American society. These writings included An Address to the Public (1789), A Plan for Improving the Condition of the Free Blacks (1789), and Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim on the Slave Trade (1790). In 1790, Quakers from New York and Pennsylvania presented a petition for abolition, supported by the Pennsylvania Abolitionist Society and its president, Benjamin Franklin. On November 18, 1785, Franklin was unanimously elected as the sixth President of the Supreme Executive Council of Pennsylvania, a position analogous to the modern role of governor, replacing John Dickinson. Franklin held this office for over three years, serving the constitutional limit of three full terms. He was re-elected to a full term on October 29, 1785, and again in the fall of 1786 and on October 31, 1787. His term officially ended on November 5, 1788, though there is some uncertainty about the exact conclusion of his tenure, as Franklin, by then aging, may not have been actively involved in the council's daily operations toward the end of his term.
